newsitem.title: USA: US House banking panel plans new bank reform bill.
newsitem.headline: US House banking panel plans new bank reform bill.

text.p: House Banking Committee chairman Jim Leach said Tuesday his committee would prepare a new bank reform bill by Friday incorporating portions of earlier proposals.
The bill would be open for any amendments and a vote at a committee session starting next week, the Iowa Republican added at the opening of a committee hearing.
Leach said he remains optimistic that the Banking Committee will pass some comprehensive financial reform proposal.
"I am increasingly optimistic that a bill can be worked out this month in this committee," Leach said.

The new bill would incorporate elements of Leach's own bank reform bill, a bill introduced by Rep Marge Roukema, New Jersey Republican, and Rep Bruce Vento, Minnesota Democrat, and a bill introduced by Louisiana Republican Richard Baker, as well as the recently unveiled Clinton administration plan.
The Banking Committee heard testimony from Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin and Under Secretary John Hawke after Leach's opening statement.
Rubin reiterated the Clinton administration's support for overhauling antiquated U.S. banking laws.
"We're still operating under an outdated legal and regulatory structure," Rubin said. "The old lines that once separated the insurance, securities and banking industries have increasingly blurred."
The administration's plan, and all three of the bills introduced in the House of Representatives, would end the 1933 Glass-Steagall Act's separation of banking from other financial services.
But the four plans each have a different approach about the possibility of going farther and allowing banks to conduct nonfinancial, commercial activities.
The Clinton plan did not take a position on the controversial question of mixing banking and commerce.
Rubin reiterated that position at Tuesday's hearing. Asked by Rep Roukema for his personal view, Rubin declined to answer.

"Let me say that my personal position and my position as Secretary of the Treasury tend to meld together," Rubin said. "I think you all are going to have to figure out, because they really are predominantly social and cultural issues, not economic issues."
